title: The first sight: an old man
hookLine: on a chariot ride with Channa he sees a man bent with age and asks, will this happen to me
carry: this is coming for all of us
tomorrow: the second sight: a sick man

lines: A PALACE WITH NO OLD FACES.
cards: A road swept clean and hung with decorations. And at the side of it, a man who was never supposed to be there. The stories say the young prince grew up without a single old face.
His father, remembering the prophecy that his son might leave and become a teacher, kept every sad thing out of sight: three palaces, music, gardens, young and beautiful people everywhere.
Then one day the prince asks his charioteer, Channa, to drive him out to the park. This is the first of four things he was never meant to see.

teach.h: WHAT IS WRONG WITH THAT MAN?
teach.b: The man is bent almost double. Gray hair, few teeth, leaning on a stick, trembling as he walks. The prince has never seen anything like him.
What's wrong with that man, the prince asks. His hair isn't like other people's. His body isn't like other bodies.
Channa answers plainly: that's what we call an old man. Then the question the story turns on.
Will this happen to me? Channa doesn't soften it. Yes.
To you, to me, to everyone. Nobody gets past old age. The prince has the chariot turned around.
No park today. He goes home and sits alone with it.

teach.h: A STORY TOLD OF AN OLDER BUDDHA.
teach.b: One wrinkle in the sources: the Pali discourses tell the four sights about Vipassi, a Buddha of long ago. Later biographies tell it of Siddhattha, and that's the version in temples and picture books today.
It echoes the Buddha's own quieter memory from the palaces: the pride of youth falling away.

teach.h: THIS IS COMING FOR ALL OF US.
teach.b: Either way, the point holds. The prince didn't learn a new fact; everyone knows people grow old. What changed is that he let it mean him.
Old age stopped being something that happens to other people. That shift, from them to me, is where Buddhists say the path begins to open.

how: Buddhists retell the four sights as the beginning of the Buddha's search, and one's own aging is the first of the five remembrances, which the Buddha said should be reflected on often.

the charioteer who told the prince that all grow old
the palace gatekeeper who kept sad sights off the road

the prince turned the chariot around after seeing the old man
no park that day. he went home and sat alone with it.

games.q: you're the prince. your charioteer has just told you that you, too, will grow old. what do you do?
o: carry on to the park and forget it.
turn the chariot around and go home to think.
order the old man taken off the road.
games.why: he turns back. no park today. the story says he went home and sat with it, and the palace's music couldn't reach him.

practice: Close your eyes, and bring to mind one old face you know well: the lines around the eyes, the hands. Let a quiet thought arrive: this face was once young like mine, and mine is on its way to this.
Hold the two faces side by side, kindly, and let any gratitude come.

wordCard.voice: Channa. The prince's charioteer, who drove him past an old man and couldn't soften the truth. The first of four sights that turned his life around.

orig.note: Pali: old age, aging. The first of the sights, and the first of the five remembrances.

carryVoice: Your line: this is coming for all of us. Not a threat: just the plain answer Channa gave. That's day thirty-one.
